title: How to work chain stitch in cross-stitch
subtitle: A linked-loop line stitch for bold outlines and decorative borders
excerpt: Chain stitch is a line of interlocked loops where each new loop anchors the previous one. In cross-stitch pieces it appears as a decorative border or a bold outline, where a single or double back-stitch would look too light for the scale of the design.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, chain stitch chapter. Weldon's Practical Needlework (1880s), Internet Archive.

glossaryTerms.definition: A line stitch made up of interlocked loops where each new loop is anchored by the needle passing through the previous one, creating a linked chain along the stitched line.

A solid outline stitch worked in a single strand along the back-stitch layer of the chart. You stitch backwards along the line one stitch at a time, each stitch finishing where the previous one started.

A stiff, evenly-woven cross-stitch fabric with clearly visible squares formed by groups of threads. The default for beginners. Counted in squares per inch: 11ct, 14ct, 16ct, and 18ct are the common counts.

The six-strand embroidery thread used for cross-stitch. Each skein is made of six strands twisted together loosely; the stitcher strips out the number of strands needed for the fabric count (two strands for 14-count Aida) and threads them together.

Come up at the start of the line. Hold the floss loosely to the side with your free thumb.

Insert the needle back into the same hole or just beside it (the entry point of the current stitch) and bring it out two to three Aida squares ahead along the line. The needle passes over the loose floss on the surface.
Pull through slowly, drawing the floss forward until a loop of even width forms. Do not pull tight enough to close the loop flat against the fabric.
For the next chain, insert the needle back into the hole at the tip of the current loop and bring it out two to three squares ahead again, over the new loose floss. Repeat along the line.
At the end of the line, anchor the final loop with a small catching stitch over the tip of the last loop, then take the thread to the back and end it in the usual way.

items.symptom: The loops are uneven in size along the line
items.cause: Inconsistent needle placement, varying between two and four squares between stitches.
items.fix: Count the same number of Aida squares for each loop before inserting the needle. Two to three squares is the standard for 14-count.

items.symptom: The chain pulls tight and the loops flatten against the fabric
items.cause: The thread is being pulled too firmly when drawing each loop forward.
items.fix: Stop when the loop width roughly matches the width of the planned chain line. The loop should sit a little proud of the fabric surface, not pressed flat.

content.text: Chain stitch works well as a frame for a small sampler or as the border on a quotes-and-sayings hoop piece. Once comfortable with a straight line, try working it in a gentle curve to see how the loops adapt.
